claims.text: The feedstock is pre-alloyed, spherical AlCrFeNiSi powder.
The proposed intervention is in situ substrate and powder-bed preheating to approximately 400 °C during selective laser melting.
The build is conducted by selective laser melting under a high-purity inert atmosphere.
The intervention is intended for miniature AlCrFeNiSi component geometries.
Mechanical evaluation will be performed from room temperature to approximately 700 °C.
Substrate and powder-bed preheating reduces thermal gradients during solidification.
Reduced thermal gradients lead to lower dislocation densities.
Reduced thermal gradients produce more controlled precipitate formation at cell boundaries.
Elevating the base temperature decreases the temperature differential between the melt pool and substrate.
The decreased temperature differential mitigates rapid contraction and associated residual stresses.
More controlled cooling minimizes non-equilibrium phase formation.
More controlled cooling promotes a more uniform microstructure that benefits mechanical performance.
Preheated components will have significantly lower residual stresses than ambient-base-temperature controls.
Preheated components will have fewer microstructural defects, including high dislocation densities and irregular precipitate distributions.
Preheated components will exhibit improved yield strength relative to ambient-base-temperature controls.
Preheated components will exhibit improved ductility relative to ambient-base-temperature controls.
Conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing without substrate preheating typically produces high residual stresses.
Conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing without substrate preheating typically degrades microstructural uniformity and mechanical properties.
The efficacy of the intervention for larger components or different alloy systems remains unvalidated.
